title: A Cellar for the Harvest
premise: Folklorist Yara Voss arrives in the isolated village of Hessel to record its harvest songs, only to find the villagers refuse to sing any verse twice — because the second singing is an invitation. When every mirror in his rented house begins reflecting the room one second late, Yara realizes the delay is a door, and something on the other side has been waiting since 1974, when the village's founding families took a child from the well-cellar as payment for a fertile harvest. The late reflections belong to that child, now grown into something ancient and hungry for memory. To survive, Yara must uncover what was taken, return it before the autumnal equinox refills the well, and choose between destroying the evidence he came to preserve or letting the village's sin be sung at last.
about_author: A. M. Eriksen is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in rural Scandinavia before turning to fiction. They write horror about what communities bury in order to prosper.

chapters.title: The Verse You Don't Repeat
chapters.summary: Yara Voss arrives in Hessel with recording equipment and academic confidence, renting the old Kessler house. At the tavern he hears half of a harvest song before the singer, Marta Ilves, stops mid-line, pale. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into unease as the whole room goes silent around him.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Yara interviews villagers, collecting fragments; each refuses to sing anything twice, some refuse to sing at all. He transcribes obsessively in the Kessler house, finding a 1974 parish ledger with pages razored out. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: the archivist's thrill shadowed by the sense that his notebook is being read by someone else.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: At dawn the bathroom mirror reflects the room a beat behind Yara's movements. He tests it with a dropped cup; the reflection drops it after. In the glass, briefly, a small handprint appears on the inside. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: rational denial cracking into cold, physical fear.

chapters.title: What Marta Almost Sang
chapters.summary: Yara presses Marta Ilves, the tavern singer, who admits the song is a 'tally' — sung once a year to count what the village owes. She warns him away from the Kessler house and the old well-cellar beneath it. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: guilt and protective terror; she recognizes the house chose him.

chapters.title: The Well-Cellar
chapters.summary: Ignoring warnings, Yara finds a bricked hatch in the cellar floor and a dry stone well shaft below, its walls scratched with tally marks from floor to ceiling. His recorder captures a second heartbeat under his own. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: dread deepening into compulsion — he cannot stop looking.

chapters.title: Reflections of 1974
chapters.summary: In the mirror, Yara watches not his own room but a past one: a woman rocking an empty cradle, men carrying a bundled child down cellar stairs. The reflections are memories, replaying on loop, one second late. POV: Yara via the mirror. Emotional beat: horrified empathy — he is watching a theft.

chapters.title: The Founding Families
chapters.summary: Yara researches parish records in the church archive and finds six family names tied to the 'Harvest Covenant' of 1974, including the Kesslers — his landlords' line. The current patriarch, Aldo Kessler, catches him reading and offers him money to leave. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: the corruption of power made visible; the village bought its abundance.

chapters.title: Aldo's Bargain
chapters.summary: Aldo Kessler confesses partially: in 1974 the harvest failed, and the six families 'made an arrangement' with whatever lives in the well. Every year since, the fields have been impossibly rich. He insists nothing was killed — 'returned,' he says, using the wrong word twice. POV: Aldo. Emotional beat: self-justifying rot; a man who has rehearsed innocence for fifty years.

chapters.title: The Child Who Was Taken
chapters.summary: Marta, breaking her silence, names the taken child: Lias Voss — a relative Yara never knew existed. His own family emigrated from Hessel the year after. The house didn't choose him randomly; it called him home. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: grief and vertigo — the folklorist discovers he is folklore.

chapters.title: Songs That Count Down
chapters.summary: Yara plays back all his field recordings and finds extra verses appearing on tapes he never edited — verses that describe him, in the present tense, descending. The song is finishing itself through his equipment. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: loss of authorship; the documenter becomes documented.

chapters.title: Mirrors Multiply
chapters.summary: Every reflective surface in Hessel now lags: windows, spoons, the river. Villagers smash their mirrors; the shards each reflect a different year of the child's captivity. The six families meet secretly; two vote to take Yara. POV: ensemble, anchored on Marta. Emotional beat: communal panic, the covenant fraying.

chapters.title: The Second Singing
chapters.summary: Someone sings the harvest song a second time — deliberately — as sabotage or summons. That night the fields bloom out of season, grotesquely, and the well-cellar fills with black water overnight. The equinox countdown begins. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: awe weaponized; beauty as threat.

chapters.title: Lias
chapters.summary: Through the deepest mirror, Yara finally meets Lias — no longer a child but a thing woven of fifty years of remembered songs, starving for a memory that isn't captivity. It doesn't want revenge; it wants to be returned, which means something worse than death. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: terrible tenderness toward the monster.

chapters.title: What Returning Means
chapters.summary: Marta deciphers the tally marks: 'returning' requires a life freely given in exchange, sung into the well by blood kin. Yara qualifies. The six families would prefer he be pushed rather than willing — willingness is what makes the harvest last another fifty years. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: love against duty crystallizing; she cannot let them use him.

chapters.title: The Archive Burns
chapters.summary: Aldo's son burns Yara's recordings and notes to erase the covenant's paper trail, but the fire spreads to the church archive — and the smoke, briefly, forms verses. Documentation was prayer; burning it was blasphemy, and the well responds. POV: Aldo's son. Emotional beat: power devouring its own heirs.

chapters.title: The Village Decides
chapters.summary: The six families convene to force Yara into the well before the equinox. Marta betrays them, giving Yara the one thing they destroyed: she sings the full song to him, twice, willingly taking the curse of the second singing onto herself. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: sacrifice as defiance; duty inverted into love.

chapters.title: Equinox Eve
chapters.summary: With the water rising and the village hunting him, Yara descends into the well-cellar carrying only his notebook and Marta's song. The reflections close around him like water. He understands at last what must be returned: not a life, but the memory — the village must remember Lias, aloud, forever. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: resolve born of clarity; fear transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: The Third Verse
chapters.summary: Climax. In the flooded cellar, Yara confronts the thing the six families bargained with — older than Lias, fed by forgetting. He offers the trade: Lias's freedom for the village's compulsory remembrance, sealed by singing the forbidden verse himself. The well takes his voice instead of his life. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: triumph at ruinous cost.

chapters.title: Aftermath, One Second Late
chapters.summary: Yara wakes mute, the mirrors still, the water gone. Lias is nowhere and everywhere — a name now carved on the parish memorial where no name was. The six families find their harvest failing for the first time in fifty years. POV: Aldo. Emotional beat: reckoning; power stripped to bare accountability.

chapters.title: The Song Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Marta teaches the village the complete harvest song, both singings, as penance and protection. Some leave Hessel rather than carry the memory; those who stay sing badly, off-key, every year, together. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: battered, imperfect communal healing.

chapters.title: What Yara Kept
chapters.summary: Voiceless, Yara rebuilds his archive from memory, writing the true account of 1974 and publishing it under the village's real name. The book is dismissed as fiction — except in Hessel, where every household buys a copy and reads it aloud each equinox. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: quiet vindication; documentation fulfilled as prayer.

chapters.title: A Cellar for the Harvest
chapters.summary: Years later, Yara returns each autumn to hear the song sung twice. In the Kessler house mirror, sometimes, a figure waves — not late anymore, but exactly on time. On the final page of his notebook, in handwriting not his own: thank you. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: peace with an open door; love outlasting duty.
